**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference Guide to Its Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass | 1.00794 u (average, weighted by isotopes) |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Periodic group | 1 (alkali‑metal group, but a non‑metal) |
| | Period | 1 |
| | Block | s‑block |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Ionization energy (1st) | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Atomic radius | ~31 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm |
| **Physical State (STP)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (−423.17 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (−434.69 °F) |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 14.304 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 25 °C) |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.449 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Heat of fusion | 0.000 kJ mol⁻¹ (negligible) |
| | Compressibility factor (Z) | ~0.9 at 1 atm, 25 °C |
| **Chemical Properties** | Bond type | Diatomic (H₂) |
| | Bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride) |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (HX → H⁺ + X⁻) |
| | Redox behavior | Strong reducing agent (forms H₂ gas) |
| | Combustion reaction | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic) |
| | Hydrogen bonding | Can act as a donor in H‑bonding (e.g., in water) |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (≈0.0006 mol L⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Very high (e.g., in hydrocarbons) |
| | Reactivity with metals | Forms metal hydrides (e.g., NaH, CaH₂) |
| | Reactivity with halogens | Forms hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI) |
| | Reactivity with oxygen | Forms water; can form hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) under certain conditions |
| | Reactivity with nitrogen | Forms ammonia (NH₃) via Haber process (requires catalyst, high T & P) |
| | Reactivity with carbon | Forms hydrocarbons (e.g., methane, ethane) via various processes |
| | Reactivity with sulfur | Forms hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) |
| | Reactivity with phosphorous | Forms phosphine (PH₃) |
| | Reactivity with noble gases | Generally inert; can form weak complexes under extreme conditions |
| **Isotopes** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant (~99.98 %) |
| | Deuterium (²H, D) | Stable, ~0.015 % natural abundance |
| | Tritium (³H, T) | Radioactive (half‑life 12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion and radiolabeling |
| | Isotopic mass differences | Affect kinetic isotope effects in reactions |
| **Applications & Uses** | Fuel cell technology | Hydrogen + O₂ → H₂O (electricity) |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen |
| | Metallurgy | Reducing agent for metal extraction |
| | Chemical synthesis | Feedstock for ammonia, methanol, etc. |
| | Medical imaging | Tracer in PET scans (tritiated compounds) |
| | Energy storage | Hydrogen storage (compressed, liquefied, metal hydrides) |
| | Food industry | Hydrogenation of fats and oils |
| | Electronics | Used in semiconductor fabrication (e.g., plasma etching) |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; wide flammability range (4–75 % in air) |
| | Explosion risk | Can form explosive mixtures with air or oxygen |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but inhalation of high concentrations can displace oxygen (asphyxiation risk) |
| | Radioactivity | Tritium is radioactive; requires shielding and monitoring |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders or cryogenic tanks; careful leak detection |
| | Environmental impact | Low; water is the primary combustion product |
| **Miscellaneous** | Quantum mechanical behavior | Exhibits quantum tunneling in certain reactions |
| | Spectroscopy | Strong absorption in infrared (stretching mode ~ 4400 cm⁻¹) |
| | Magnetic properties | Diamagnetic (no unpaired electrons) |
| | Phase diagram | Only one solid, one liquid, one gas phase under normal conditions |
| | Standard enthalpy of formation | ΔH°f (H₂(g)) = 0 by definition |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation | ΔG°f (H₂(g)) = 0 by definition |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and (in its most common form) one neutron.
- **It is a diatomic gas** at room temperature and pressure, with extremely low density and high diffusivity.
- **Chemically, it is highly reactive**: it forms a wide variety of compounds (hydrides, acids, organics) and is a powerful reducing agent.
- **Its isotopes** (protium, deuterium, tritium) give it unique roles in nuclear fusion, medical imaging, and isotope labeling.
- **Safety**: While non‑toxic, hydrogen’s flammability and potential for explosive mixtures demand careful handling.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
